title: Saddleback Church and the Montgomery Bus Boycott
coreMove: Turn private agreement into visible participation routines carried by strong ties, weak ties, and peer expectation.
sourcePressure: The Montgomery bus boycott and Saddleback Church show that movements need social habits. Strong ties help launch action, weak ties scale it, and repeated group expectations make participation feel normal enough to continue after the spark.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version credits movements to charisma, outrage, or viral messages alone. The writer must show the social structure that makes participation repeatable.

hook: A viral post creates a movement overnight.
A vague community meeting with no participation routine.
counterintuition: Most people think movements are about passion, but actually...
Treating private agreement as collective action.
Reducing social habits to abstract belonging.
tryThisNow: Set a timer for ninety seconds and text everyone you know.
Post a public callout and wait for virality.
Ask people whether they care without giving them a visible repeated role.

exampleSpecs.domain: tenant elevator-repair campaign in a high-rise
exampleSpecs.audience: a tenant organizer whose neighbors complain privately but skip public meetings
exampleSpecs.stakes: elderly residents remain trapped upstairs if complaints never become visible pressure
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The organizer starts with two neighbors who check on each other daily, then puts a floor-by-floor repair ledger by the mailboxes so weak-tie neighbors can see signatures accumulating and feel expected to add theirs.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: An elevator inspection sticker curls beside a row of mailboxes.

exampleSpecs.domain: warehouse heat-break policy campaign during summer shifts
exampleSpecs.audience: a veteran picker trying to move coworkers from grumbling to coordinated participation
exampleSpecs.stakes: workers keep getting dizzy on the line because everyone assumes someone else will speak first
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Before the routine, complaints vanish at the time clock; after it, each crew pins a heat card to the shared board after break, making participation visible across friends, acquaintances, and supervisors.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A warped time clock sits beside a blank heat-break board.

exampleSpecs.domain: farmers market vendors organizing accessible stall placement
exampleSpecs.audience: a vendor with one loyal aisle group but little reach across the whole market
exampleSpecs.stakes: disabled shoppers will keep finding blocked paths unless isolated sympathy becomes a market-wide expectation
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The vendor can complain to the manager alone, but instead stamps each stall map after a neighbor clears one path, so nearby friends start it and distant vendors see the stamp as the new norm.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A stall map is smudged with rain near a stack of folding tables.
mustAvoid: private agreement with no public routine

exampleSpecs.domain: basement music venues adopting hearing-protection norms
exampleSpecs.audience: a drummer who wants more than a one-night safety announcement
exampleSpecs.stakes: regulars and openers are damaging their hearing because earplugs still signal weakness in the scene
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The drummer asks two close bands to put earplug tins on their amps first, then gives every visiting band the same soundcheck line until the weak-tie touring groups copy what the regulars visibly do.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A tin of foam earplugs rattles on top of a guitar amp.

exampleSpecs.domain: rural clinic patients coordinating rides to keep a route open
exampleSpecs.audience: a patient advocate whose clients agree the shuttle matters but cancel alone
exampleSpecs.stakes: the county will cut the route if ridership looks too low for another month
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: The advocate predicts reminder calls will not be enough, then creates a weekly ride board where church friends, cousins, and waiting-room acquaintances can see who has claimed seats and who still needs a partner.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A shuttle timetable is taped beside a clinic waiting-room window.

exampleSpecs.domain: coastal town campaign against illegal river dumping
exampleSpecs.audience: a fish-house owner trying to connect dockworkers, parents, and weekend volunteers
exampleSpecs.stakes: private outrage will fade if residents do not get a repeated way to show up before the next permit hearing
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: After a small hearing fails, the owner replaces one-off speeches with a Friday sample-tag handoff: close dock friends collect first, parent groups carry the tags to storefronts, and weekend volunteers sign the delivery sheet.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: A stained test strip dries on a fish-house counter.

skillTargets: separate strong-tie launch work from weak-tie scaling work
identify participation routines that make private agreement visible and repeatable
spot movement plans that rely only on charisma, outrage, or virality
evaluate whether peer expectations are specific enough to carry action after the initial spark

tryThisNowSpec: Name one cause people around you privately support. Write one strong-tie starter, one weak-tie bridge, and one visible weekly act that would make participation expected.
